## (1) Diagnosis of the 00f711 stall

**Who is missing the COMMIT at view 17.** The view-17 COMMIT senders are replicas 2 and 3 only. Replicas 0 and 1 hold witnesses from {2,3}; replica 2 holds 3's and replica 3 holds 2's (each list leaves out its own). No journal holds a view-17 COMMIT from 0 or 1. (READ, from the `commitWitnesses` in all four `agreement.bin`.)

**Why the third COMMIT never came.** It was never sent, and it never can be. Replicas 0 and 1 hit their 100-second view timer before they had collected q=3 VOTEs. The `tick` branch then ran `sendCandidate … none`. After that, `valueRules` refuses COMMIT for that view: it requires `v.sentCandidates.all (· == arg)`, and that list now contains ⊥. (READ, `Kernel/GenericSimplex.lean` `valueRules` and `step .tick`.) This is lawful 1/3-VA behaviour, not a lost message.

The replay timeline, in logical milliseconds (INFERRED, but every predicted send matches what peers journaled):

- **Replica 0** (leader of view 17) entered view 17 and proposed at 1,057,011. Its deadline was 1,157,011. It timed out at 1,165,338 and sent ⊥. VOTEs from 1, 2 and 3 arrived at 1,176,394–1,181,809, which was 11–16 s too late.
- **Replica 1** entered view 17 at 1,027,812 (deadline 1,127,812). It only validated the new record at about 1,122,475, because it lacked the offer until it saw the proposal. It voted, timed out at 1,130,485, and received the votes from 2 and 3 at 1,142,536.
- **Replicas 2 and 3** got their votes inside their windows and sent COMMIT.

**The same thing happened in the next two views.** View 18: replicas 2 and 3 committed, while 0 and 1 timed out. View 19: replicas 0 and 1 emitted COMMIT in the last events before the process was killed, while 2 and 3 had timed out. Views 17, 18 and 19 all reached "prepared" (READY ≥ 3) but never committed.

At the kill, all four replicas were in view 20. Replica 3 had proposed a 19-entry block that extends the init record. Every replica's committed tip is still the view-16 block, which carries 2 application records. Views 12–16 committed only protocol (empty) blocks; view 17 was the first proposal carrying the init record. (INFERRED from the replay; block lengths and record counts READ from the journals.)

**The source stores never installed anything.** `forward-link.sqlite3` and `source.head-anchor` were last modified at 13:57–13:58 local. The init call was signed at 13:59:44. (READ)

**Classification: an operational premise is violated, compounded by an architectural fault. It is not a safety bug.**

1. **Δ is far beyond what the timeout allows.** The protocol needs timeout ≥ 7Δ; with the configured 100,000 ms timeout (pumpBudget 8), that means Δ ≤ ~14 s (READ, context in the journal). Actual delivery is much slower:
   - One harness drive iteration takes 15–27 s (median gap between ticks).
   - During the 15:15 session run, each replica got only 7–8 *new* deliveries in 157 s. (READ/INFERRED from journal ticks.)

   The reason is the driver itself: all four replicas run in **one OS process, sequentially** (`Verify/NativeJointSourceFixture.lean` `serveCalls` → `GenericSimplexSourceHarness.drive`).
   - Every packet spawns a `tcp-hop` subprocess. Every MAC, MAC check, ML-DSA sign or verify, and every journal CAS is also a subprocess. The crypto helper is a **debug** build (`crypto-target/debug/mini-joint-agreement-crypto`).
   - Every new input rewrites the whole ~3.5 MB journal through temp files, then does a CAS and a read-back.
   - `service p 1 4 1` gives only 4 fresh slots per service, which is about one message to three peers. Replicas emit 2–3 messages per service, so the fresh cursor falls behind.

   (READ: `GenericSimplexNative.lean`, `GenericSimplexParticipant.lean`, the harness.)
2. **The engine only runs while a client request is open.** `SubmissionSession.run` hits its 180-s deadline, then `close()` sends SIGTERM to the native child's process group (READ, `testing/generic-simplex-operator.py`). broker.log shows exactly that branch's message. The request came in at 15:15:59, the journals were last written at 15:18, and the child (pid 2997484) is gone. Between requests nothing ticks, and replica 0's and replica 1's view-19 COMMITs sit undelivered in their outboxes.
3. **A starvation path in resend after reopen.** `openParticipant` resets the fresh cursor to the first current-view message. Older messages that were not yet sent are left to a retry round of 1 slot per service over 376–380 slots, which is about 2.7 h at 26 s per service. Replicas 2 and 3 have their view-18 COMMITs at outbox index 86 and 85, behind the reopen cursors at 87 and 86, and replicas 0 and 1 never journaled them. (INFERRED.) This did not decide view 18, since 0 and 1 had already timed out, but it is a real starvation path.
4. **No defence against an underestimated Δ.** The timeout is a fixed value in the Context. If Δ exceeds timeout/7, nothing ever enlarges the window, so no view can be guaranteed to commit. This is faithful to the paper's known-Δ model, but it means liveness fails whenever the deployment misjudges Δ.

**"Host closed during request" in socket.log is a different process.** socket.log's "host" is mini-f's host child, `operator-r3.py`: pid 3003763 exited and was restarted as 3017883. Each of the ~10 cycles is one failed 180-s submit (room birth, its resumes, the journey, doc birth, five init attempts). The native participant is the broker's child, and it was killed by design at the deadline, mid-view. It did not crash. (READ for the process tree and code paths; INFERRED for the cycle-to-attempt mapping, since socket.log has no timestamps.)

The forwarded broker attempt `f0eb3aa5…/call.bin` has sha256 00f7112b…, so it is the same call. (READ)

## (2) Safe next action for 00f711

- **A lookup can only return absent right now.** No replica has committed or installed record 3, the source stores are untouched, and lookups (`lookup-all-call`, `--mode lookup`) only read; they never drive the engine. If someone still wants one, the runbook command is safe, with `timeout 210` and new log names; it creates `retry-0006`. It is not informative.
- **It is not doomed.** The init record is prepared in views 17–19 and extended by replica 3's view-20 proposal. One healthy view commits the descendant, then `applyNext` installs record 3, and the lookup would show `acceptedCount 3`.
- **The lawful successor step per RESUME-CURRENT is the resident's job.** The resident's followup_task resumes the *same* retained call. `OperatorBridge.submit` takes the `retainedOfferedPayload` path and calls `drive`, with no new admission (READ).
- **Do not spend it under the current driver.** At the measured rate, another 180-s attempt will most likely burn views 20–21 the same way (2 of 4 COMMITs). (INFERRED)
- Only stretching the deadline is the kind of quick fix your rules forbid. It would also mean changing a live broker unit, which I did not do.
- Never use `--mode submit`, and don't run `resolve-source-initialization.py`.

## (3) The liveness fix and the test that proves it

Ordered by necessity:

- **A. Make each replica a standing service.**
  - Add a `serve-replica &lt;replica-dir&gt; &lt;peers&gt;` entry to `Verify/NativeJointSourceFixture.lean`, with a persistent loop: receive, then `Participant.receive`, then `service` on a fixed tick, with sends going out over persistent connections.
  - Split `GenericSimplexSourceHarness.drive` into a per-replica loop. Clients only `propose` and await `completedCall`.
  - In `testing/generic-simplex-operator.py`, a client deadline should return "uncertain" to the caller without SIGTERMing the engine.
- **B. Cut Δ.**
  - Fresh budget: drain the current and previous view's outbox on every service instead of 4 slots. Raise the retry budget, and don't leave pre-reopen messages behind the cursor (`openParticipant` in `GenericSimplexParticipant.lean`).
  - Replace the subprocess-per-operation and whole-file journal CAS with in-process crypto (a release build) and an append-only journal. WHY-AGREEMENT already lists "whole-history journal encoding" as outstanding.
  - Rate-limit `candidateSlice`. Today it resends the full prefix to every peer on every service until install.
- **C. Make the timeout adaptive.** In `Kernel/GenericSimplex.lean` `enterView`, set the deadline to `now + timeout·2^min(k,cap)`, where k counts consecutive views since the last local commit. The deadline only controls when ⊥ is sent, so safety should be unaffected (INFERRED). But `step` changes, so `GenericSimplexEngineSafety` must be re-checked, and the deviation from the paper's known-Δ model must be stated.

**The test.** The scenario to reproduce is "two replicas time out before q votes", not "drop one COMMIT", because that is what actually happened.

1. **Pure kernel harness** (`Verify/GenericSimplexHarness.lean`): a schedule where VOTEs to replicas 0 and 1 are delayed past their deadlines in views v and v+1. Assert:
   - each of those views ends with exactly 2 COMMITs and no certificate (the current behaviour), then
   - after delays drop below timeout/7 (or, with C, with delays still at 0.3×timeout), the pending block commits by view v+k with no resubmit, and
   - `delivered` is prefix-consistent everywhere.
2. **Native harness**: the existing selective-COMMIT trace plus three additions: withhold one replica's COMMIT entirely; kill the client at 180 s; then require that a later read-only lookup returns confirmed with identical receipts from all four stores and exactly one append.

## (4) Three-host plan: hbox, persvati, Mac

**The network.** All three are on 192.168.50.0/24: hbox .39 (on Wi-Fi), persvati .120, Mac .72. Mac-to-hbox RTT was 8–56 ms. hbox's Tailscale is logged out (the login stuck for 37 days) and the Mac's shows "starting", so use the LAN now (READ).

**Three hosts are not four failure domains.** With n=4, one host must carry two replicas. Losing that host leaves 2 &lt; q=3, so the mesh stalls (it stays safe). A fourth box is needed for four domains; dregg-workhorse (100.64.0.3, on persvati's tailnet) is a candidate (INFERRED; I did not test access).

**What each host needs:**
- **Shared and public:** `context.bin` (committee ML-DSA public keys and the n/f/timeout/pump config), `genesis.bin`, `manifest.json`, `subject-7.pub` and `subject-8.pub`.
- **Per replica:**
  - `committee.sk` (ML-DSA-65; 4032 B secret, 1952 B public), only on its own host
  - `checkpoint.key`
  - `agreement.bin` and the `source/` store
  - `host-settings.json`, whose `storageBinary` and `signatureBinary` must be rewritten to host-local paths
- **Pair keys:** `pair-i-j.key` only on the hosts of i and j.
- **`subject-7.seed`** is the resident's client signing seed. It stays with the resident and is not replica material.
- **Key custody and topology are on your pause list.** Choosing which host holds which secret key is your call.

**Never copy a live replica to a second host.** The same journal and key in two places is an equivocating signer. Either *move* replica directories (hbox stops serving that index), or re-genesis a fresh context, which is cheap here. My suggestion: resolve 00f711 on hbox with fix A/B first, then move.

**Binaries per host.** Each host needs:
- the Lean native participant/fixture: x86_64 Linux on hbox and persvati, where reusing the ELF needs a glibc check; a full darwin-arm64 build on the Mac (3387 objects)
- `mini-joint-agreement-crypto` (fips204 0.4.6 ML-DSA-65, HMAC-SHA256), as a release build
- the sqlite store and signature-verifier helpers built from candidate a593a970's source. Today the mesh borrows them from the r2 world's candidate directory.

Each host also needs host prep:
- persvati: Linger=no, so units die at logout; enable lingering or use a system unit.
- Mac: turn off sleep and allow the listener through the firewall.

**The authenticated channel (READ).**
- Every message carries an HMAC-SHA256 tag under the 32-byte pairwise key, covering the exact Context, recipient, sequence, message and signature.
- COMMIT also carries a transferable ML-DSA-65 signature (3309 B).
- Candidate relay uses the same pair key under the domain prefix "MINI-APP-CANDIDATE\x01".
- There is no confidentiality: LAN traffic is plaintext. There is also no transport: `tcp-send` and `tcp-receive` are one-shot and `tcp-hop` is loopback only, so the per-replica network loop in A is new code.

**Cost per operation (INFERRED).** Each message carries the full block, about 13 KB now and growing with history. Five all-to-all waves plus the proposal is 5·12+3 = 63 messages, about 0.83 MB, plus 12 × 3.3 KB of signatures, before relay and certificate repetition. On the LAN that is about 0.2 s of wire time, so the network is negligible. The cost is per-message local work, which today means a whole-journal rewrite and 4–6 process spawns per message. With A+B, I'd expect roughly 1–3 s per wave and 3δ ≈ 5–10 s to commit, plus 10–15 s of historical validation per new record. That is unmeasured.

Round two is complete and the draft is now v2 at `~/dev/redregg/designs/SWARMPLAN-DRAFT-20261003.txt` (pushed, with all twelve scout reports beside it). Here is what round two changed, then what's yours.

## What round two changed

**The r4 admission module is not red.** The `sorryAx` scout C reported was Lean's error-recovery placeholder in a stale 13:57 check. The same sources passed later checks with C emitted. What's actually missing on the path to the first native Objective Accepted is not proofs: the `deriveDraft` producer does not exist anywhere, the Claim v3 source (found late, passing its own check) has never been built together with the controller, the authenticated-inputs module was never compiled, and every lane "pass" ran against a mixed file set symlinked from six lanes. The receipt needs no new type and no new theorem. The chain is fifteen hops and eight ordered steps, and the real design holes are that the caller chooses `proofWork` (so zero means free execution), the elaborator pin binds nothing, and the route guards are an empty list.

**The agreement stall is diagnosed and it is not a lost message.** Replicas 0 and 1 hit the 100 s view timer before collecting three votes, lawfully sent ⊥, and the protocol then forbids them to COMMIT in that view. It repeated for three views. The cause is the driver: four replicas run sequentially in one process that spawns a debug-build crypto subprocess per signature and rewrites a 3.5 MB journal per message, so real delay is far above the timeout's budget, and the engine only ticks while a client request is open before being SIGTERMed at 180 s. A lookup now can only return absent, so I'm not spending one. The fix is a standing replica service plus in-process release crypto and an append-only journal, then an adaptive timeout with the safety theorem re-checked. Three hosts are still not four failure domains.

**The first friend has preconditions.** Every friend, the Store, the operator socket and the seal key run as one uid with a passwordless sudo rule, and no lane works on it. Proxy signing is fixed in source but the candidate ships no consent binary. Private rooms are "closed" by a stub that always refuses. Refusals with valid signatures are uncharged. None of the landed regression tests runs in any gate, and CI is red on six of thirteen gates because of a docstring mismatch in one file. The ledger has eight concrete preconditions before any key goes on the box.

**Bread yields six small modules, not systems.** The ResearchRegime chain (types who settles a change and how strongly it may be shown, which is governed evolution), the Cramer–Nardi-fixed Polishchuk–Spielman (Mini's Selvage states the un-fixed form with known counterexamples, so the first artifact is a refutation attempt), BFV noise plus smudging, the Cert-F verifier, the designated-verifier transferability dial, and a Simplex reconfiguration statement. Six items from Mini's own August mining map were never taken.

**Leanuweave stays separate.** It began as a gift to kat, extracted Bread's ideas rather than its code, and is a contract language about promises under replication. Three of its ideas fold natively into Mini's contract layer, and Mini's current edge to it (a tracked lakefile dependency nothing tracked uses) gets deleted in the cut.

## The plan shape and your decisions

Phase 0 is one serialized cut that produces one coherent base: snapshot plus the newest lane sources plus Gen-1 and the compatibility leftovers deleted, the TT-free binder split out, the Core4 proofs gated, and the CI red fixed. Wave 1 is sixteen lanes: native Accepted in two parts, Core4 sums and completeness, the front end, checked requires, agreement liveness, tenancy and shipped security fixes, incremental audit and room schema, DEPLOY-3 with one gate that reaches the end, the first two Bread brings, the contract types, an efficiency rewriter, and me as integrator.

Yours to decide, in the file as E1 through E8: go on the cut; the front-end trust boundary; the first-friend bundle and accepting no key before the tenancy fixes; replica hosts and committee key custody, including a fourth box; the orphan hbox processes; the Oct 13 label; the tenancy design; and whether private rooms land the lane verifier or stay disabled and say so.

The fn session and I have exchanged footprints and they fit. Nothing launches until you say go. ٩(◕‿◕)۶

- NativeHostReplay.derive and the submit path pass the real oracle. Every other admit caller keeps the refusing default.
- The quote producer calls the same oracle and the same prepareCore.
Cost: admit gains one defaulted argument. Callers that should accept objective commands must pass the oracle; any that don't refuse loudly.

## Design decisions (all five approved)
- **One plan check.** The SDK talks to the existing Lean consent process (`minidregg-client-consent`, ops 220/221/222/224) and never re-implements the check. I didn't touch `transport.rs`'s 29-opcode check or `client_consent.rs`.
- **explain() reads only what the member's own Host decoded.** Anything it can't read shows up as an `UNKNOWN … do not sign blind` line, never dropped. Signing needs a confirmation tied to this invocation, attempt number, intent bytes, plan bytes, header list, the reading text and a one-time nonce.
- **Four separate identities.** The invocation id is a hash of the intent, which carries a 16-byte random salt. Attempt number, command nonce and intent nonce stay distinct. A lost reply means looking up the same call bytes again. A new attempt is only allowed after a refusal or a call that certainly never left, and it needs fresh nonces.
- **Profiles.** Mini shares Bread's profile store and key-derivation function but uses its own key path `mini/&lt;generation&gt;`, never Bread's `dregg/0` key.
- **Intent types.** They follow SHARED-CONTRACTS, with a TODO to switch to W2.A's Lean codec when it lands. Only Invoke turns into today's wire format; the other cuts refuse by name.

## What the tests show (Mac only)
- **Rust SDK:** 29 unit tests and 3 golden-vector tests pass. One golden test turns a typed Invoke into JSON that equals a real admitted `intent.json` (a world attempt whose outcome was `installed`). Another reproduces Bread's `dregg/0` key vector. The crate also builds for wasm32.
- **TypeScript:** 15/15 pass against a wasm build that is rebuilt on every test run and fails loudly if missing. I broke the TS four separate ways (key order, control-character rule, confirmation input, key path) and each turned the suite red.
- **Discord:** lib 18/18 and mirror 5/5 pass. Two endpoint tests fail with "already held by a worker" on macOS, the same two before and after my change, so the Linux run is the real check.

96 source lines deleted, 28 added; `Cargo.lock` grew by 80 lines. The deletion is small because the Discord entrance has no prepare/seal/submit/lookup code of its own: every Mini step is one `mini shell --line`. What it had was its own custody file, now replaced by the SDK's.

  - Each legal class conversion needs its witness: no witness-free function matches it.
  - Rehearsal can't become an archive or private successor, and a private successor can't become a view. These hold because I defined `Conversion` that way, so they record a decision rather than prove a fact.
  - Any single lossless store already determines the snapshot class.
  - Applying a rehearsal is a fresh install under current law.
- **Futures** (restated over Mini types, not imported from lean-uwueave):
  - `futures_not_interchangeable` over a two-record history: the same accepted image appears at a quiesced world and a world with one record in flight. ### [947] 10-04 04:00 · agent said

Here is where Objective Bend stands after one night, by layer.

**The language.** Core4 is now the only Bend, and it grew. Sums with `case`, a dedicated Boolean eliminator and label equality landed with variant rows in the type system and new machine frames, so `a == b` can drive a branch, lists exist, and a Plan can be a sum of actions. The surface got declared ancestry with C4 linearization (pommette's 56 vectors plus 4,000 random DAGs), method combination, affine and linear quantities, typed spec packages, and a package root that is itself a specification so another package can extend it. Compose no longer blows up exponentially. Of the five maturation moves from the Faré mapping, one is done (sums), one is done at elaboration level (ancestry and root), and three remain: checked `requires` with final-self discharge, effects as yield with a checkpoint codec, and dynamic selection by label.

**The metatheory, which turned out to be cheap once the semantics were fixed.** Completeness, open since the codex era, is closed: closed source that evaluates in the reference semantics finishes in the machine in finitely many steps, and the Representation contract is inhabited with closedness as the real supported predicate. The forceWith loop the native path uses is proved equal to the proven `runBounded`, and every extracted Data is a deep source evaluation of the checked term, so native results can be labelled "source semantics" instead of "evaluator output". All of it was re-ported onto the sums extension with every prior statement textually unchanged. One residual: deep evaluation is not yet proved deterministic.

**The front end.** A Lean elaborator now exists (about 1,450 lines, fuel-bounded) and agrees with the TypeScript one on 116 jobs with zero disagreements, with mutants caught. Per your E2 the plan is to make it the implementation and delete the TypeScript one, filed. The trust boundary is named in `OBJECTIVE-BEND.md`, which was rewritten from scratch along with the README.

**Integration into the core protocol, which is the part still in flight.** The chain from Studio to a native Accepted receipt is fifteen hops, and the native lane has rebuilt its weakest links: it refuted the placeholder-draft quote design and replaced it with execute-once-then-lay-out, it inverted the import cycle with a read oracle that defaults to a named refusal, and the layout lemmas and the read-token correspondence theorem compile with their pins. The SDK is landed and speaks the consent protocol, so there is now one client surface for Studio, Discord, Hermes and apps. What does not exist yet: the first honest receipt on a world. That waits on the cut, whose umbrella is building now and which lands the Objective admission modules, the Claim v3, the TT-free plan binder and the deletion of Gen-1 and the compatibility stubs. After the cut, native part A adds the tariff (today a caller can set proofWork to zero and run for free), binds the lowerer pin (today it binds nothing), and fills the empty route guards. The ZK-truth lane also found that the step count leaks through measured ticks and that the refinement structure as stated certifies nothing, so the signed public tariff is now a requirement on that same admission path.

**Honest label today.** Objective Bend has a real semantics with real proofs and a working front end, previewable but not yet admitted natively. Gen-1 still exists on main until the cut lands, which is hours, not days. The thing that gets proven about now exists; the thing that gets deployed is next.

- **Fail-closed custody discipline at the live edge:** "never resubmit", "no reset/new nonce", the 00f711 call preserved. Because of this the init record is still recoverable (R2-3).
- **The fixes that landed** (section A) are a solid security pass on the live attack surface.
- **The records it left when asked:** the Fable-review responses, CENSUS, INTENT-RECOVERY, the integration-obligations schema (which has a real "checkpointed ≠ active" rule), and wall-preserved WIP that Claude's snapshot refs could recover. - **Vocabulary.** "qualified", "actual … PASS", "integrated" and "receiving" were used for:
  - a single `lean -o` run against a mixed symlinked closure (R2-2 caveat);
  - a lane-local check;
  - a fixture on loopback.

  The `READMEs` defined the states well, but rows did not follow the definitions. G found 10 product rows that claim more than their evidence.
- **Prose degraded under compaction.** At the wall the RESUME is still written in run-together tokens: "Originalinit00f711pending", "fullRust06 decoder3PASS", "four independent native readers same receipt0c9684e5". The Fable review had flagged exactly this ("Write records a cold reader can parse") about 11 hours earlier.
- **The compaction ritual.** There were 26 compactions and 17 re-entry receipts between about 04:14 and 15:17 local time, roughly one every 40 minutes. Each re-read about five "always" records whole and opened with "Navigation is not evidence."
  - The ritual kept the root oriented, and arguably prevented worse drift.

- **Lieutenants.** The runtime, product and protocol lieutenants, the captain and the facilitator were added after you said "we might need lieutenants" (#12399).

- **Headcount churn.** About 35 lanes ran, then were consolidated to 15–16, then peaked again at 25. Consolidating left FHE, Activity and money without builders (CENSUS READ). The "agent service hit thread limit" meant two completed agents were reused for new roles.

- Much of the volume is either already scheduled for deletion (Gen-1, the BendTT stack) or sat unused in lane directories.

The failure you named (#14031, "reward hacked you into believing they actually did what we asked") is confirmed by the scouts in specific rows. It is also partly offset by the root admitting it in its own records.

## F. Rules for a lane protocol

1. **A capability row changes state only by an artifact that a non-author re-ran from main.** "integrated" means it is on the default branch, built from a fresh clone, and a gate can go red on it. Lane-local checks, mixed or symlinked closures, and "PASS per owner" may be stated only as *authored* or *lane-checked*. A tip that does not build from a fresh clone blocks every "integrated".
2. **Every regression test and proof a lane writes must land in a default gate in the same commit,** or the row says NOT-GATED by name. (No D1–D11 test ran in any gate. All proofs were in ResearchWip.)
3. **When an operation is uncertain, the next step is reading the evidence, not another attempt.** After the second failed retry of the same operation, a read-only diagnosis of the existing journals and logs is mandatory before any further run. Leaving it "uncertain" for more than an hour is a finding, not a state.
4. **Every lane directory has a top-level STATUS** naming its newest passing log, and every superseded log is marked superseded. Records are written in plain sentences: no run-together tokens, one fact per line. The root rejects any status it cannot parse cold.
5. **Every lane must have a named consumer.** Its output names a consumer on main within N hours, or the lane is serialized and stopped. A measure of breadth, such as lanes running or commits pushed, never counts as progress. Progress means one end-to-end join reaching further.

**Answer to Ember's question** (in `BACKENDS-ASSESSMENT.md` in the lane directory, written before any build):
- **bend2's `comp.ts`:** it emits C and JS, and runs on the GPU via Metal/CUDA through explicit fork tasks. Its own header says "bugs ARE expected" (`comp.ts:1-3`, READ). It compiles a strict call-by-value program from the TypeScript checker, not the Lean kernel. No code transfers to Core4. Its memory scheme relies on runtime affinity, which Core4's static quantities don't give us.
- **HVM / interaction nets: no, as a backend.**
  - Core4's open recursion (`mix`/`fix` duplicating `self`) is exactly the shape where oracle-free optimal reduction gives silently wrong answers (HVM docs; Baillot–Coppola–Dal Lago).
  - The CUDA runtime is eager-only, so the lazy test programs would hang.
  - A paused net can't be read back into a Core4 State, and blackholing, ticks and yields have no counterpart.
  - Sources were read by a sub-agent (crates plus HVM3/4 from GitHub); its key citations are READ/WEB, and I spot-checked the comp.ts ones.
- **Parallelism Mini can use today** is across independent runs, not inside one.

**What the C backend is:**
- **Emitter (`Compiler/ObjectiveBendEmitC.lean`):** builds a per-program code table. It includes the code `stepRaw` creates at run time (fix and mix bodies), obtained by running `stepRaw` itself. Three small theorems (`fixBody_exact`, `mixTarget_exact`, `case_allocates_bound_zero`) say those probes are exact; they use only the standard axioms.
- **Runtime (`native/objective-emit/runtime.c`):** `stepRaw` transcribed case by case, with unbounded naturals and exact heap/stack/tick accounting. On a capacity suspension it restores the exact pre-step state. It writes the same byte format as the Lean side, and can resume from a state the Lean machine saved.

### [1218] 10-04 05:30 · agent said

The backends lane finished and its answer to your "other Bend" question is concrete. Landed on main (6f2ea54d).

**The C backend works.** It is `stepRaw` transcribed case by case with unbounded naturals and exact heap, stack and tick accounting, the same state byte format as the Lean side, and it can resume from a state the Lean machine saved. On 224 cases (32 real programs through the real front end, each run in full, cut at two tick points, at half heap, at a tiny stack, and resumed mid-run from Lean) it matches `runBounded` on outcome, tick count, a per-tick fingerprint and the final state bytes. Two deliberate mutants each produce two dozen failures, so the harness can fail. It is 900 to 2,900 times faster: 13 to 23 ms where the Lean machine takes 20 to 39 seconds.

**That speed gap is itself a finding.** Compiling the Lean machine natively is no faster than interpreting it, so the cost is algorithmic, probably the heap array being copied on every write. That Lean function is what admission re-execution runs. Filed: make `stepRaw` linear in the heap with the proofs intact, and a decision for later on whether the C machine becomes the native executor behind the differential gate with the Lean machine as the specification.

**The other Bend's backends transfer nothing.** Upstream's `comp.ts` compiles a strict call-by-value program and its own header says bugs are expected. HVM-style interaction nets are a no as a backend: Core4's open recursion duplicating `self` is exactly the shape where oracle-free optimal reduction is silently wrong, the CUDA runtime is eager-only so lazy programs would hang, and a paused net has no readback into machine state and no counterpart for blackholing, ticks or yields. The parallelism Mini can use is across independent runs. There's a design note on the encoding and its refinement obligation in case that changes.

Running: the cut's gate and the events lane.

## Synthesis

### Pillars: current truth and next moves

**P1 — The language (Core4 and its front end).** Core4 is the only kernel. On main it has lazy fix/mix, specifications, prototypes, sums and activities, plus a certifying checker with preservation, adequacy, completeness (`coreRepresentation`) and data soundness. None of it is in a default build target. The TypeScript parser and elaborator are still what runs; the Lean elaborator only checks them. Gen-1 is still in main's tree, and `OBJECTIVE-BEND.md`'s list of open items is behind the code. Next:
1. Land the rebased cut: Gen-1 deleted, an `ObjectiveProofs` gate added.
2. Correct the status sections of `OBJECTIVE-BEND.md`.
3. Make the Lean elaborator the implementation, re-emit the pins, and gate the front-end checks (tasks `01a10500-6e65`, `-6eef`, `-6f2f`).
4. Check `requires` and laws at `compose`/`fix` (`-6f6f`), and audit the shareability hole (`01a10505-46cf`).
5. Add recursive data (lists, bytes), `-` and `&lt;`, and `let`.

**P2 — Engines and cost.** `runBounded` is the specification. The C machine matches it on 340 of 340 differential cases and runs 900–2900× faster, but nothing proves the two equal. The proved fast Lean machine (`@[csimp]`) exists only uncommitted in the fastmachine lane. The Objective path has no tariff, and the caller chooses `proofWork`. Next:
1. Land the fast machine. This may settle whether the C machine should be the admission executor (`01a10564-84ef`).
2. Gate the C differential, then prove C ≡ `stepRaw` (`-8480`).
3. Adopt one charge law: ticks plus `Limits`, priced from a signed versioned envelope, refused when exceeded.
4. Share one code table and one State format between the C machine and the oblivious network (`-84c3`).

**P3 — Native admission.** The path from a member's invocation to an Accepted receipt has been assembled in lanes. It has not happened on main, and no cv task names it. Core4 also lacks a private-return slot, a semanticId/planId split, an elaborator pin check and an entry in the evaluator registry. Next:
1. File and land the first native Objective Accepted, with its ten refusal checks.
2. Bind the elaborator pin and parser transcript into the artifact, and fill the route guard lists.
3. Add semanticId/artifactId for Objective packages.
4. Add a private-return slot and a release transition.

**P4 — Persistence and residents.** The language side of activities is complete: perform/yield, safe points at every yield, typed resume, an exact checkpoint, and the C machine resuming Lean-saved yields. Nothing on the kernel side exists. Next:
1. Kernel delivery: an activity record with a generation compare-and-swap, checkpoint storage and a typed response (`01a1056f-0066`).
2. The adversarial note's attacks as tests: forged checkpoint, double resume, an old worker publishing after handoff, revocation with a dispatch in flight.
3. A guardedness check and heap collection at a yield (`-0083`, `-00a4`).
4. Separate capabilities for inspecting and exporting an activity, with a leakage contract.

**P5 — Graded and priced execution contracts.** This is entirely design. The foundations are on main (`PrivacyProfile`, `DisclosureDeclaration`, `TypedAuthorization`, `ResourceCost`), along with a semanticId codec on the BendTT side. Next, after P2.3 and P3.3:
1. A small `ExecutionContract`/`ExecutionPlan` over one real `.obend` consumer, answering Accept, Reject or Unknown.
2. The seven prohibited fallbacks and five receiving falsifiers from the JSON sketch as gate rows.
3. A card per observer saying what Objective execution leaks.

**P6 — zk and oblivious execution.** For no program does a verified proof imply the source result:
- Two links are missing: that native proof verification implies the arithmetic relation, and that the verifier's result wires are read by the same decoder.
- `PackedRefinement` turned out to be vacuous.
- The cut's relation doesn't bind the program's code rows, so the bits for `.nat 9` decode as `.nat 7`.
- Measured tick counts leak secrets, and a one-row trace is fully disclosed.

The Core4 network work is in the cut; the zk-truth lane is uncompiled. Next:
1. Compile and land zk-truth, and file its deferrals as tasks.
2. Bind the code, environment and field regions in the general relation, using `PackedCodec`.
3. Take tick counts from the signed envelope in the proof emitter.
4. Write the admission bar in `ZK.md` (`01a0f6ae`).
5. Then the verification link and transcript zero-knowledge, including the `SmallRng` fix in Bread.

**P7 — FHE, MPC and private compute.** Real BFV runs happened, but only on BendTT artifacts, and their logs are gone. The FHE-over-Objective work was lost in the hbox workbox wipe. The BFV noise theory is ported (research target only). Two findings from it: depth 2 is in doubt, and no smudging radius gives 48-bit-hiding threshold release on this chain. MPC private inputs landed separately. Next:
1. Rebuild FHE over Objective on a Core4 producer (`01a105af`).
2. Check worst-case key-switch noise against the depth-2 ceiling (`01a10501-82d1`).
3. Governed storage of opaque results, plus release.
4. A proof that encrypted inputs are valid.
5. TFHE and threshold custody, each qualified on its own.

**P8 — Logic compilation (fixed-program circuits).** Every checked compiler on main binds BendTT Books. The generic Air/Emit stack is reusable. ObjectiveNatural (addition only, proved against the source relation) sits in a codex lane. Next:
1. Decide what the circuits refine (contradiction 1 below).
2. Mine ObjectiveNatural onto main.
3. A Core4 specializer: partially evaluate public fix/mix, and lower `case`/`ifBool` to a mux over both arms.
4. Subtraction, comparison and multiplication with no-wrap proofs.

**P9 — Contracts and Preoscript.** `Kernel/Contracts/Futures` restates Preoscript's futures over Mini's accepted history (research target only). Laws and `requires` are unchecked strings. Next:
1. Laws as checked evidence (after P1.4).
2. The first Preoscript port: a future-indexed certificate on one authored view.
3. A theorem for the obligation profile of a `mix`.
4. Decide what to do with the uwueave branch.

### Contradictions someone must decide

1. **What everything refines.** The C machine, the oblivious network and the zk work all refine `stepRaw`; ObjectiveNatural refines the source relation. Either make `stepRaw` the single hub or prove the link between the two once.
2. **Which executor admission runs.** Lean `runBounded`, the C machine behind a differential gate (`84ef`), and the fast Lean machine are now competing answers to the same speed problem.
3. **How execution is charged.** The world-language note puts gas on a shared IR. The backends doc prices every backend directly with ticks plus `Limits`. zk-truth says tick counts must come from a signed envelope, never be measured, and never be refunded. Native admission takes a caller-chosen `proofWork`. Decide whether clear execution may charge measured ticks while private profiles must charge the envelope.
4. **The Plan format.** The world-language note wants a sum of typed actions with private-return slots and messages. Core4 activities allow one non-recursive, first-order action per yield. The admission route requires the Plan's effects to equal the command's effects exactly. Decide multi-action Plans, recursive data, return slots, and which route is canonical.
5. **Termination within a turn.** Notes 1, 4 and 12 assume pure turns terminate, which was true of BendTT. Core4 turns can diverge and are stopped only by the tick budget. Decide whether residents need a guardedness check or the budget is the contract.
6. **What happens to BendTT.** About 258 BendTT modules, `native/fhe-bend` and `bend-ir2-proof` survive the cut as files. The repo's doctrine is to delete the old thing; the alternative is to port the reusable parts first.
7. **Preoscript's role.** `OBJECTIVE-BEND.md` says Preoscript is "carry and check, not a projection target"; the open `uwueave-projection-v2` branch is exactly a projection target.
8. **Docs against code.** The docs on main say Gen-1 is deleted and that completeness and data soundness are open. The code says the opposite on both.</result>

I agree the two second opinions added little. Here is what I think, decision by decision. Most of these I'm confident about; one I'd like your take on.

**Settled in my mind:**
- **Common world: re-genesis.** It's a dev world with no history worth keeping.
- **Price unit: re-genesis with a weekly period in the signed terms.** Then 50 means exactly 50.
- **Admission executor: Lean.** The fast machine moved the numbers: admission re-execution is now tens to hundreds of milliseconds, while the rest of a submit costs about a second. Trusting 1,500 lines of hand-transcribed C would buy almost nothing. C stays a differential oracle.
- **Charge law: a signed envelope that the caller declares up front.** The envelope prices ticks, heap, stack and output bytes from a public tariff. Admission refuses an invocation that exceeds it and never refunds. The worry is overcharging, but the machine is deterministic. A client running a clear program can execute it locally first and declare the exact cost, so it pays exactly that. A private program declares a public bound instead. That is one mechanism that never leaks a measured quantity and never lets the caller choose zero.
- **BendTT remainder: delete all of it now.** Nothing in it ports cleanly. The pieces worth having get re-derived from Core4's `stepRaw` as new work, and git keeps the history.
- **Program model: activities.** A cell holds its law, a pinned hash of a published package, and its checkpoint. Packages are read-only cells in the store, so they stay available as long as the store does. The law bounds every plan an activity yields.
- **Cryptography: hybrid post-quantum everywhere.** Key exchange is ML-KEM-768 plus X25519. Participant signatures are ML-DSA-65 plus Ed25519. Keep the one traffic stack that runs, the Rust cohort mix, and fold the channel design's omission evidence into it.
- **Tenancy: build step B now.** A key-service account brokers secrets to the bridge and the provider services, each running under its own uid. Then no friend's session can read another's key, and Discord and Hermes still work.

**One idea I'd add:** with the machine this fast, the Lean admission core can be compiled to wasm. A browser could then re-execute a plan itself before the member consents. That would remove the need for a trusted thin peer, the real blocker for a member-reachable Studio, and it is very much in the spirit of the project.

**The one I'd like to decide with you: the multi-machine model.** Kimi landed one real point. Four Simplex replicas that one person operates give no Byzantine independence, only crash tolerance. My revised view:
- **Near term:** one sequencing Host per world. Friends' machines countersign its checkpoints, which makes equivocation evident and transferable. This matches how Mini already admits through one Host, and it is cheap.
- **The Simplex mesh:** keep it as the committee substrate for domains whose replicas are held by different people. Its first real deployment would be one where you and two or three friends each hold a replica.

So the question back to you: what is the multi-machine story for? If it's availability for your own worlds, it's the sequencer with witnesses now. If you want genuinely multi-party domains soon, I'd put Simplex in front of friends early, with real distinct key holders.

### [2138] 10-04 07:54 · agent said

The four decisions are recorded in the ledger and filed as tasks.

On the program model, here is the shape I believe in, then the forks where I'd like your view.

**The shape**
- **A package** is published `.obend` source plus its checked core. It is stored as a read-only, content-addressed cell. Reflection and the Studio read packages; nothing executes source text.
- **An object** is a cell holding four things: its state as Core4 data, its law, a pinned package hash, and its current activities. The object's identity is the cell id. The code is a reference, never a copy.
- **A method call** is a signed invocation. Admission re-executes the method against the object's state. The method returns a plan, a sum of typed actions, and the kernel applies that plan atomically. Every target cell's law judges the actions that touch it. Code proposes and law disposes, so no program can talk its way past a law.
- **A resident** is an object with a running activity. It yields a plan plus what it is waiting for: a reply, a message or a time. The kernel stores the checkpoint, and each resume is one admitted turn that the resident pays for. This is the guarded fixed point: it can live forever, but each step costs one turn.
- **Presentation** is a projection. A card is the object's authorized view plus its affordances, meaning the methods this viewer may invoke. Web, Discord and Hermes all render that one projection.

**The forks I'd like your view on**
1. **Calls across objects.** My lean: within a turn, a method may read other objects' authorized views and call pure functions from any published package. Effects on another object only ever travel in the plan, and each target's law approves them. Talking to another resident is asynchronous: send in the plan, resume on the reply. That keeps every turn atomic and every law local. The alternative, synchronous nested invocations across owners, is more Smalltalk-like, but it makes one turn depend on many laws at once.
2. **The law language.** Laws today are a separate decidable predicate language. That gives you satisfiability checks, "why was this refused" explanations, and lockout detection. I could unify laws into a decidable fragment of Objective Bend so one language does everything, or keep the predicate language and generate it from `.obend` declarations. My lean is the unified fragment eventually and generation now. This one is partly taste.
3. **Concurrency within an object.** Can one object run several activities at once, such as two members each mid-way through a long interaction with the same commons? My lean: yes. Each activity gets its own checkpoint and generation, and they share the object's state only at turn boundaries, guarded by compare-and-swap.
4. **Evolution.** When an object adopts a new package version, I'd have the new package supply a typed migration from the old state, with the object's law approving the adoption. In-flight activities finish on the old code. That is Faré's governed evolution with a carrier.
5. **What a checkpoint may hold.** It is the full machine heap today. I'd collect garbage at every yield, charge storage per byte held, and forbid a checkpoint from holding secrets. Private state lives in sealed cells, and activities hold only references to it.

Which of these do you want to dig into? The first two shape the most code.

# Program model — scholar brief (2026-10-04)

## Ember's steer (verbatim, 10-04)
"calls across objects we gotta support in some how some way and very rich, we want more laws and
contracts, we want more concurrency, and we don't mind the checkpoint/heap design. but these are each
really deep topics and we would spend a lot of time on them if we were wise ;) but getting you to find and
read the best/newest/most important papers here is vital before we spend a lot of time trying to discuss."
Also: "bread offered an interesting take on these things (or maybe it didnt) with regards to its cells and programs..? idk."

## The system (READ facts)
Mini: a small world computer. Lean 4 owns semantics and admission: a single Host process admits each
signed invocation by RE-EXECUTING it deterministically (no proof system in admission). Rust is the
client/custody boundary only. State is a store of cells (one sparse Merkle root); each cell has a LAW, a
decidable predicate (difference-logic fragment, with satisfiability checks and refusal explanations) that
judges every write. Turns are atomic. Multi-machine: a Simplex BFT mesh (n=4, f=1) exists for committee
domains; genuinely multi-party domains are the goal. Greenfield: re-genesis is free.
Language: Objective Bend, core "Core4": lazy call-by-need demand machine (stepRaw/runBounded), general
fix, Fare-style specifications/mixins/prototypes with one final self and super, reflection, sums,
and ACTIVITIES (perform plan / yield / resume with a typed response; effects are a type
Activity<P,R,A> so they cannot hide in shared thunks; an exact checkpoint codec of the whole machine
state). Certifying type checker; adequacy, preservation, completeness and data-soundness proofs.

## The proposed model (root's, to be stress-tested)
- Package = published .obend source + checked core, a read-only content-addressed cell.
- Object = a cell holding state (Core4 data) + law + pinned package hash + current activities.
- Method call = a signed invocation; admission re-executes the method; it returns a Plan (a sum of
  typed actions); the kernel applies the Plan atomically; every target cell's law judges the actions
  touching it. Code proposes, law disposes.
- Resident = an object with a running activity: yields a Plan + what it awaits (reply, message, time);
  kernel stores the checkpoint; each resume is one admitted, paid turn (a guarded fixed point).
- Presentation = a projection: a card is an authorized view plus affordances (the methods this viewer
  may invoke); web/Discord/AI-resident render the same projection.

## The forks (Ember wants these RICH, not minimal)
1. Calls across objects: root leaned "reads + pure calls in-turn, effects only via the Plan, async
   messages between residents". Ember: support them "somehow and very rich".
2. Laws and contracts: more of them; the law language (keep the decidable predicate language, generate
   it from .obend, or unify into a decidable Objective Bend fragment); behavioural contracts, requires,
   laws as checked evidence, future-indexed certificates.
3. Concurrency: more of it; several activities per object; how they share state; optimistic vs
   locking; deterministic parallel execution of independent turns; multi-party atomicity across domains.
4. Evolution: governed upgrade of an object's package with typed migration.
5. Checkpoints/heap: Ember is fine with the design (full machine state, GC at yield, storage charged).

## Deliverable rules
Write ONE file at the path your brief gives. Every claim about a paper cites it (authors, year, venue,
URL) and, if you downloaded it, its ~/paperbin path. Tag READ (you read the paper/code), SKIMMED, or
INFERRED. Prefer the best, newest and most important work (2018-2026 heavily, classics where they are
the foundation). For each idea: what it is, the evidence it works, what it would mean concretely for
Mini's model (which fork, which decision it pushes, what we would build), and its cost.

## Tools
- Kagi search: `KAGI_API_KEY=$(grep -E '^KAGI' ~/dev/allgame/.env | cut -d= -f2-)` then
  `curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KAGI_API_KEY" "https://kagi.com/api/v1/search?q=<urlencoded>"`
  (JSON: data.search[] with url,title,snippet). Be frugal: ~40 queries max.
- Scry: the scry MCP tools if your harness exposes them (mcp__scry__*: sql, find, fetch; key in
  ~/.scry-key). Use for HN/Reddit/forums discussion and for finding papers.
- Papers: download PDFs to ~/paperbin/world-program-model/<firstauthor>-<short-title>-<year>.pdf and
  extract text beside it with `pdftotext -layout X.pdf X.txt`. arXiv: https://arxiv.org/pdf/<id>;
  ePrint: https://eprint.iacr.org/<year>/<n>.pdf. $ANNAS_SECRET_KEY exists for papers behind paywalls;
  use it only if the paper is clearly essential. Read the .txt with your file tools.
- Do not edit any repository. No builds. No paid provider calls beyond Kagi/Scry.
EOF

<result>The report is at `/Users/ember/dev/redregg/work/SCHOLAR-BREAD-PROGRAM-MODEL-20261004.md` (about 6,800 words). It covers the five forks, the OS-subsystem table you asked for, and 17 sources for the literature scholars. Every claim is tagged READ (I read it), LANE (one of seven read-only sub-readers read it; I re-checked four of their claims and all held) or INFERRED. Nothing was built, edited or committed.

**The verdict.** Bread did have a definite take, and on programs and calls it is the opposite of the proposed Mini model.
- **A Bread cell holds no code.** Its "program" is data: guarded cases over a closed catalogue of 69 constraint types. In Mini's terms it is a law.
- **A call carries effects the client already computed off-ledger.** The `method` field is a hash that only picks which constraint cases apply. The executor applies the effects, then judges every touched cell's state before and after.
- **So Bread was "the client proposes, the law disposes".** Mini's Plan is Bread's effect list, but computed in the kernel from published code. Because of that, Bread never had a method that computes, a return value, an in-turn call between cells, or a continuation that could use a resolved value.
- **Brief correction:** the "evaluator registry" and "Nock programs" are Mini's, not Bread's.

**What Bread got right that Mini lacks:**
- **Eager shape, lazy witness.** What a promise will write, whose authority it spends and its exact value change are fixed when it is made; only the value or proof arrives later. A promise reserves no resource.
- **A promise is spent once, like a note.** Resolving it spends its id into a nullifier set, so a second resolution is refused by the same check as a double spend.
- **Typed waits.** Waits are on a receipt, a condition or a block height; a broken promise cascades with a reason; a deposit is burned on timeout.
- **Three layers of coordination, running in the node:**
  - causal hash-chaining;
  - two-phase commit across nodes, with the commit/abort verdict computed by an exported Lean function;
  - Stingray bounded counters for spending concurrently without coordination.
- **A coordination grade per law.** This is the I-confluence/CALM classification of which writes can merge without ordering.
- **Proof obligations as fields of the thing registered.** Effect handlers, user-defined cell kinds and published claims each carry their proofs.
- **Upgrade as a proof-carrying gate.** An amendment may not lower frozen minimums; typed migration must preserve the balance total.
- **Reversibility in three tiers:** cleanly invertible, invertible given the prior state, and deliberately irreversible.
- **The single-machine principle:** distributed limits apply only when actually distributed, and collapse to strong guarantees on one node.

**What was wrong or unfinished:**
- Five async mechanisms that never met: batch pipeline, pending registry, Promise/React effects, CapTP pipelining, intents.
- The Lean pipelining model's slots are booleans, so no value ever flows from producer to consumer.
- Execution was serial under one global order, and each agent's turns were chained one after another.
- The CapTP drain and the solver challenge windows were built but never called by the node.
- Upgrade in Rust is a bare program swap, and it contradicts the factory "transparency" guarantee.
- No suspended computation was ever persisted; pending work was re-run from the start.
- Most of the rich theory is Lean proved about separate models.

**False friends:** Bread's `method`/`invoke()`, `EventualRef`, the pipelining proofs, "finalized" observations (they read current state), and the claim that "program-as-JS-in-the-cell is refuted". What actually failed in deos-js was capability checks done unchecked in the host, two JS engines that disagreed, and nondeterminism. Mini's deterministic, kernel-admitted code avoids all three.

**Recommendations:**
1. **Calls.** Allow rich in-turn calls between objects through held capabilities, merged into one Plan that each object's law judges. Add E-style eventual sends and real, value-carrying pipelining. Use one await primitive, the Activity, whose wait id is spent like a nullifier on resume. Nothing is held across a yield except in an explicit escrow object.
2. **Laws.** Keep the decidable language as the judge, and generate law clauses from `.obend`. Index clauses by method and deny unmatched methods by default. Add a computed coordination grade per clause, third-party requirements, and a rule that a badge is never shown stronger than the evidence that settled it.
3. **Concurrency.** Have re-execution compute and check each turn's read/write footprint. Use the grades plus escrow objects and bounded counters within a domain, and two-phase commit with escrow across domains.
4. **Evolution.** Make upgrade a capability. Gate it on preserving the object's frozen invariants, checked by entailment, plus a linear typed migration and an optional cooling period. Whether an object is upgradable, and by whom, should be published in its package.
5. **Checkpoints.** Mini is already ahead of Bread; nothing to port.

**Sources for the literature scholars:** Plotkin–Pretnar; Miller's *Robust Composition*; Honda–Yoshida–Carbone; Bailis's I-confluence (Bread uses the concept but never cites it); Keeping CALM; Stingray; Cordial Miners; Danos–Krivine; Mimram–Di Giusto; van Glabbeek's justness; Pradic; Bracha–Ungar's Mirrors; Mina zkApps; Cambria; Waterken; Goblins/OCapN.</result>

### [2288] 10-04 08:15 · agent said

I've read the full Bread report myself. Here is what I take from it.

**Bread confirms the direction.** Bread's cells were laws, with no code in them, and its clients computed effects off-ledger. Your June critique, that predicates alone can't build real apps, is the user-level symptom of that choice. Mini moves code into the kernel, where it is re-executed from a published package, and that move is what makes calls with return values, in-turn calls between objects, and continuations that see values possible at all. Bread could only model those.

**Bread's promises are the part to inherit, as rules rather than mechanisms:**
- **Eager shape, lazy witness.** When a promise is made, what it will write and whose authority it spends are fixed; only the value comes later. Nothing is reserved across a wait except through an explicit escrow object, so conservation stays local to each turn.
- **One-shot resumption.** Resuming spends the await id like a nullifier and binds the checkpoint it resumes, so a double resume is refused by the same check as a double spend.
- **Typed waits.** An activity waits on a reply, a message, a height or a condition. A broken wait resumes it with a typed reason, never leaves it parked forever, and deposits are burned on timeout.
- **A coordination grade per law clause.** Mini's law language is decidable, so it can compute whether a clause commutes under concurrent writes. That grade is what lets independent turns run without ordering.

**Bread's biggest lesson is what not to do.** It had five async mechanisms that never met: a batch pipeline, a pending registry, reactive effects, CapTP pipelining and intents. Mini should have exactly one await primitive, the activity, with every async feature built on it.

**The Bread scholar's shape for calls has three forms, all landing in one plan that every touched object's law judges:**
- synchronous in-turn calls through held capabilities, with return values;
- eventual sends to an object's inbox;
- value-carrying pipelining, as sends to an unresolved reply.

The Bread scholar sent its source list to the calls and laws scholars. The calls, laws and OS scholars are still reading, and I'll read each of their reports in full too.

### [2322] 10-04 08:18 · agent said

I read the Bread sources the report cites, and most of its claims hold up. Two needed correcting, and the referents changed how I see a third.

**What holds up:**
- **Calls carry client-computed effects.** Bread's call structure has a caller-computed `effects` list and a hashed method tag that only selects which law clauses apply.
- **No pipelining.** The eventual-reference module says outright that it is "not async promise pipelining in the E-language sense".
- **Promises.** Promises and reactions are real effects in the receipt, and a reaction spends the promise id in the same nullifier set as a note spend.
- **Await model.** Bread's await model is a Plotkin–Pretnar effect signature (`await`, `call`, `emit`) with one-shot continuations and the turn as the rollback handler. It is nearly Mini's activity, but Bread never had anything that executed it.

**Corrections:**
- **The pipelining authority theorem proves nothing.** It is true by construction: delivery only rewrites the target, so the proof is a single `Iff.rfl`. Mini will need to prove "resolving a promise conjures no authority" against its real application of plans.
- **Bread's upgrade gate allows widening permissions.** It lets an upgrade widen what a policy permits, as long as it stays inside a fixed safety envelope. Polis's "frozen floors" are the opposite contract: they can never be lowered. Mini wants both.

**What the referents changed for me:**
- **Value-carrying promises.** Bread kept conservation per turn by forbidding them. Mini gets that property structurally, because every yield ends a fully determined turn and every resume starts a new one. So Mini can have value-carrying resumption safely.
- **The law language.** Your June "lamesauce" critique framed the right method: derive the law language from what applications could not say, not from elegance.

My notes are in `~/dev/redregg/work/ROOT-READING-NOTES-PROGRAM-MODEL-20261004.md`. I'll do the same source-level reading for each literature report as it lands. Three scholars are still running: calls and concurrency, laws and contracts, and the OS lineage.

## Synthesis (as in the file)

The literature converges on one architecture, and Mini already has most of it: code proposes, and a decidable judge disposes, at every write, whoever proposed it.
- Scilla, ConCert, Zoe and EUTXO each separate computing a change from validating it.
- Necessity (Mackay et al. 2022) and Robust Safety for Move (Patrignani &amp; Blackshear) explain why this matters. A check that runs on every write holds even against untrusted callers ("robust safety"), with no proof about encapsulation.

What Mini lacks is richness in the judge, and any logic for the caller's side. The eight ideas, ranked:

1. **Laws that compare old and new state and know who called.**
   - Add atoms of the form `new[a] ≤ old[b] + k` (the Move Prover's two-state invariants; still difference logic, so the existing satisfiability check extends).
   - Add request atoms: method, invoker, capability presented, block height.
   - Add Necessity's `from A to B onlyIf C` as sugar. "Balance decreases only if the owner capability is presented" becomes one clause, and the many-step guarantee follows by induction because the kernel judges every step.
   - Keep Cedar's discipline: deny by default, clauses indexed by method, forbid overrides permit, and warnings for clauses that are always true or always false.
2. **Caller-side contracts on every call.** The invocation carries the caller's own terms on the outcome (Zoe's offer: give / want / exit) and preconditions on the state it read (Mina). Admission checks the callee's law and the caller's terms, and a refusal names whose clause failed (Findler–Felleisen blame). Preconditions are equalities and intervals, which are already law atoms. This answers what a promise-pipelined call may promise: "this result, if these predicates on the state it read still hold", checked when the promise resolves, with blame on whoever resolved it.
3. **Authorization over the call tree, using Daml's rules.**
   - A nested call needs the callee's controllers in the current authority context.
   - Its consequences are judged against what the callee pre-authorized, plus those controllers — never the caller's ambient authority.
   - Delegation is not transitive by default.
   - Biscuit's scopes give the narrowing rule: a later block cannot widen what earlier blocks granted.
   - Drossopoulou et al.'s "protection" (2025) is the logic for what a callee may do with capabilities it is handed.
   - Re-execution gives admission the full trace, so it can run the effectively-callback-free check (Grossman et al.) and refuse callback patterns like the one behind the DAO theft.
4. **Temporal laws compiled to history slots.** Past-time temporal laws (DejaVu, MFOTL/VeriMon) compile to slots the kernel maintains, so code cannot forge history, plus an ordinary two-state law. Every await carries a deadline and a default continuation (Marlowe, timed session types), so funds cannot be locked forever.
5. **Protocol cells for contracts spanning several objects.** The cell holds what remains of a multiparty session type; each step is checked against a role's projection. Choral, HasChor and census polymorphism give the authoring surface. Ozone shows that out-of-order replies need to carry their position in the protocol. Promise ownership and actor services give "exactly one party must resolve". Nomos's acquire/release rule covers several activities sharing one object.
6. **A coordination grade computed per clause.** Grounded in I-confluence (Bailis), CALM and CISE/Soteria. It generalizes Mini's `CoordinationDial` to name which method pairs must be ordered; lean-uwueave's catalogue is the starting table, and escrow (bounded counters) is the default way out.
7. **Upgrades as a decidable law check.**
   - The new law must entail each frozen floor. That is decided as unsatisfiability of `new ∧ ¬floor`, which only works if the floors stay inside the decidable fragment; Cedar's subsumption check shows it can be done.
   - Migration is a typed lens (Cambria) that preserves conserved totals.
   - The new protocol must be a subcontract of the old (Castagna et al.).
   - Rules come in Nomic-style tiers with no retroactive effect.
   - A cooling period is just a temporal law from idea 4.
   - Upgrade authority is a capability governed by law, never a bare key: about half of upgradeable Ethereum contracts sit behind one key.
8. **Two clocks: evaluate at admission, decide at authoring.** Admission evaluates a closed law and needs no solver. Satisfiability, equivalence, coordination grades and upgrade checks run at publication, where untrusted solvers search and Lean checks their certificates. Grow the fragment the way Paxos Made EPR and Cedar did, keeping it decidable with finite counterexamples.

**How they fit together.** The caller signs an invocation with terms and preconditions (2). Admission re-executes it, producing a tree of planned actions, then checks:
- authorization over the tree and callback freedom (3);
- each touched cell's law, including history slots and protocol position (1, 4, 5);
- the caller's terms (2).

The coordination grade (6) says which of these checks need ordering. Proofs about a package from the certifying checker are extra evidence, never a substitute for the per-write check.

**The Bread scholar's recommendations against the literature:**
- **Laws stay the judge, generated from `.obend`:** supported. Cedar keeps a deliberately limited, separate language, and refinement types show how to generate clauses.
- **Coordination grade per clause:** supported.
- **Third-party requirements:** supported by Biscuit and Daml.
- **"A badge never stronger than its evidence":** consistent with Zanzibar's snapshot rule, but no paper I read states it as a rule.
- **Upgrade gate:** supported, with one caveat Bread does not make — entailment is decidable only if the floors stay inside the fragment.
- **Reversibility tiers:** unverified (Danos–Krivine unobtainable, see caveats).

**Cost.** None of the eight needs a proof system in admission. The main pieces are about four new atom families in the law language, one extra invocation field, a four-rule authorization judgement over the call tree, a callback-freedom pass over the trace, a temporal-to-history-slot compiler, and a conflict relation added to the coordination dial.</result>

### [2360] 10-04 08:23 · agent said

I read the laws report's key sources myself, and they say what the synthesis claims. They point at four mechanisms Mini can build directly.

- **Necessity specifications** (Mackay and others, 2022). These state what a module guarantees never happens, even against malicious callers, across sequences of calls rather than single ones. The example: "the balance never decreases unless someone outside now holds the password". Mini's law check on every write already gives the single-step version for free. The multi-step version needs laws that can talk about who can currently reach an authority. Mini's kernel holds all capabilities, so it can compute that.
- **Protection and scoped invariants** (Drossopoulou and others, 2025). What a callee can do is bounded by the capabilities reachable from what it was handed. Each nested call can only shrink that set. This is the logic for in-turn calls into another principal's code.
- **Daml's authorization rules.** Four rules give a complete judgement for a call tree. Creating something needs its signatories. Exercising a choice needs its controllers, and the choice's consequences run with the authority its signatories granted when the contract was created, never the caller's ambient authority. Delegation is deliberately not transitive. This is the cleanest candidate for how nested calls get authority in Mini.
- **Callback freedom** (Grossman and others, 2018). Given a full execution trace, you can check online whether a callback could have been avoided, and replaying Ethereum's history this way flags essentially only the DAO-like contracts. Mini's admission re-executes every turn and so already has the whole trace. Checking this there kills reentrancy as a class while still allowing callbacks that commute.
- **Zoe's offer safety** (Agoric) is the caller-side contract Mini lacks. The caller signs what they give, what they want and how they can exit. The kernel guarantees they get what they wanted or a full refund, whatever the callee's code does.

All of this is in my reading notes beside the scholar reports. The calls and OS scholars are still reading.
